title: why Indian kids touch their grandparents' feet
hook: a child bends to an elder's feet, and a hand comes down on the child's head
carry: bow to what came before you

segments.voice: Yesterday: shanti, three times over. Today, a gesture you may have seen at a family gathering.

A grandmother walks in, and before anyone says hello, a twelve-year-old bends down and touches her feet. Her hand rests on the child's head for a second. Then everyone goes back to arguing about dinner. From the outside it can look like bowing to a boss. Inside the gesture, something goes both ways.

Pranam is Sanskrit: pra, forward, and nam, to bend. To bend forward, a respectful greeting. It shares its root with namaste. Touching the feet has its own name, charan sparsh: charan, the feet; sparsh, a touch. One common explanation: the head is the high point of a person, where the pride sits, and the feet have walked further down the road than yours. The high point of you meets the low point of them. Then the other half. The elder's hand comes down on the head: an ashirvad, a blessing given back. Respect goes one way, a blessing comes the other, and nobody walks away smaller. An old law book, the Manusmriti, says four things grow for the one who greets and serves elders: length of life, learning, good name and strength. Read it as a promise or as a description. Either way, the gesture says nobody invents themselves.
screen: `PRA — FORWARD. NAM — TO BEND.` · `CHARAN SPARSH.` · `A BLESSING, GIVEN BACK.` · `FOUR THINGS GROW.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Bring to mind one person who made your road easier: a grandparent, a teacher, anyone, living or not. As you breathe out, bow your head to them a little, for real. Stay down for one more breath.
Pranam. To bend forward: a bow to the ones who walked first, and a blessing that comes back. Fifth word.
Your line: bow to what came before you. Somebody walked the road first. That's day five.

story.title: the bow before the battle
story.text: On the morning of the great war in the Mahabharata, with both armies ready, Yudhishthira takes off his armor, puts down his weapons and walks alone toward the enemy's lines. His own side thinks he's surrendering. He isn't. He goes to his great-uncle Bhishma and his teacher Drona, who are fighting against him, bows to their feet, and asks for their blessing. Bhishma tells him that if he hadn't come, he would have wished him defeat. Because he came, he blesses him instead.
